newsitem.title: UK: Major's election statement in full. [CORRECTED 14:50 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Major's election statement in full. [CORRECTED 14:50 GMT]

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major announced on Monday the election would be held on May 1.
Following is the full text of his statement to reporters on the steps of 10, Downing Street, his official residence -

"I would like to formally confirm that I have seen Her Majesty the Queen this morning and sought her permission for a dissolution of Parliament and a general election on May 1. Her Majesty has consented to that. I would expect prorogation of parliament within a few days, formal dissolution in early April. Parliament will reassemble on May 7 (corrects from April 7) for the election of the speaker and the swearing in of members and the queen's speech will begin on 14 May.

Over the last 18 years we've seen a very dramatic change in the lifestyle of people in this country. There's been a revolution in choice in opportunity and in living standards. At the general election there's a choice between the party that has brought that revolution about and the two parties that have opposed almost every single aspect of those changes.

It would be ironic indeed if those parties that have opposed all the things that have brought us to our present standard of living would pretend themselves that they are capable of carrying them forward.

At the election there will be a quite distinct choice of policies between the major parties. We have set out some very clear, long-term policies to deal with almost every aspect of concerns of people in this country -- health, welfare, education, law and order as well as sustaining the most secure economic conditions we've known in this country in a very long time.
These are the matters that will be of debate, I hope detailed and careful debate and discussion, throughout the general election in every part of the country.

Also of course is the significant question of constitutional change. I am not opposed to appropriate changes in the constitution. Indeed in the past five years we've made a number of constitutional changes, perhaps more in many respects than most predecessor parliaments.
But I believe that some of the constitutional changes proposed by our political opponents are dangerous and need to be exposed for the perils that would lie ahead were we to go down that route.
May 1 is, of course, the anniversary of the coming into force of the Act of Union (grouping the countries that constitute Britain).
I have, like I guess most of you, waited a long time for this general election. I am delighted we've now got it, I'm looking forward to it.

I'm looking forward to getting out of Whitehall and Westminster and campaigning in every part of the country and taking the message of what we've achieved and of our hopes and our ambitions for this country out to people in every part of the UK.
Elections, some people say, are tough and gruelling businesses. Well, up to a point that's true.
But I think they are also a lot of fun and I am looking forward to going up and down the country taking the message that I believe is right for this country to everyone.
